objectives: Name the five senses and say what each one does.
Explain how the eyes and the ears send messages to the brain.
Describe how the nose and the tongue pick out smells and tastes.
Show how the sense of touch protects your body.
Carry out a simple test of one of your senses.
Say how to look after your eyes, ears, nose and tongue.

sections.body:
Your senses are the ways your body finds out about the world. You use them every second of every day, so quietly that you do not notice them working.

There are **five main senses**. Each one has a special job and a special organ that does the job.

**Sight** uses your eyes. You see light, colour, shapes and movement.

**Hearing** uses your ears. You hear sound, from a whisper to a jet engine.

**Smell** uses your nose. You notice smells, and you also use them to find food and to know if something is going wrong.

**Taste** uses your tongue. You taste sweet, salty, sour and bitter, and you feel hot and cold with it too.

**Touch** uses your skin. You feel pressure, pain, heat and cold, and you feel how soft or rough a thing is.

All five send messages along nerves to your **brain**, and your brain works out what is going on. Without senses, the world would be dark, silent and empty.

Your senses can be helped or spoiled. Too much loud music tires your hearing. Too little light makes your eyes work harder. A cold that blocks your nose takes away most of your taste. And there are more senses than five, like the sense of where your body is in space, but five is where every story starts.
examples: You see with your eyes, and you hear with your ears.
Your nose finds smells and your tongue finds tastes.
All your senses send messages to your brain.
sections.heading: What the Five Senses Are

sections.body:
Sight starts with light. When light from an object enters your eye, it lands on a screen at the back of the eyeball. That screen is called the **retina**.

The retina sends the picture along the **optic nerve** to the brain. The brain turns the picture the right way up and the right size. So you do not really see with your eyes. Your eyes collect light, and your brain does the seeing.

Your eyes work hard all day. They make tiny movements to look around, and they blink to keep the front of the eye wet and clean. Blinking happens without you deciding it.

Two eyes are better than one because they see slightly differently. Your brain compares the two pictures. That is how you judge how far away something is. It is called **depth perception**.

The eyes need looking after. Reading in dim light makes them work harder, and it can give you a headache. Sitting too close to a screen for hours is tiring. Look out of the window every so often, and let your eyes rest on far-off things.
examples: Light lands on the retina at the back of the eye.
Your eyes collect light, and your brain does the seeing.
Looking at something far away lets your eyes rest.
sections.heading: How Your Eyes See

sections.body:
Your ears hear by catching vibrations in the air. Sound is really a vibration, and these vibrations travel through the air until they reach you.

The vibration hits the thin **eardrum** at the end of the ear canal. The eardrum moves, and three tiny bones inside your ear pass the movement along. Inside the ear, a spiral organ called the **cochlea** turns the movement into nerve signals. The brain hears them as sound.

Your ears protect themselves. Small hairs inside the ear help push dirt away. And loud sounds make you flinch before you even think about it. That flinch is your body warning you that the noise is too strong.

Your nose works by chemistry. When you breathe in, the air carries tiny bits of things into your nose. The smell cells inside pick them up and send the news to your brain.

Your tongue is covered with tiny bumps called **taste buds**. They pick out sweet, salty, sour and bitter. The tongue also feels hot, cold and pain, because those are the same nerve endings as touch.

And here is a surprise. Most of what people call taste is really smell. When your nose is blocked by a cold, your food tastes flat, even though it has not changed at all.
examples: Sound is a vibration that travels through the air.
Taste buds on your tongue pick out sweet, salty, sour and bitter.
When my nose is blocked, my food tastes flat.
sections.heading: How Your Ears, Nose and Tongue Work

sections.body:
Touch is the sense you use the most, and you notice it least. It works all over your skin, and it never stops.

Your skin has different nerves for different jobs. Some tell you about a light touch. Some tell you about a firm push. Some tell you that something is hot, and others warn you that it is too hot. Some send the sharp message of pain.

Pain is not a punishment. It is a warning that something is hurting you, so you can stop before it hurts more. That is why it is dangerous to ignore pain.

Your hands are the busiest part of your touch system. They have a very fine sense of texture, so you can tell silk from sandpaper with your eyes closed. They also know where things are without looking, which is called **proprioception**.

Touch tells you about the world, but it also tells you about yourself. It tells you that your arm is in a different place now. It tells you when you are cold, and it warns you before you touch something hot.

And touch is not only for skin. You have touch sensors in your mouth, in your nose and in your fingertips. When you press a key on a keyboard, you feel it, even if you do not look.
examples: Different nerves in your skin tell you about touch, heat and pain.
Pain is a warning, not a punishment.
Your hands know where things are without you looking.
sections.heading: How Touch Keeps You Safe

sections.body:
These are the words you will need when you talk about your senses.

A **sense** is one way your body finds out about the world. You have five main ones.

**Retina** is the screen at the back of your eye. Light lands there and the picture begins.

**Optic nerve** is the nerve that carries the picture from your eye to your brain.

**Cochlea** is the little spiral inside your ear that turns vibrations into nerve signals.

**Taste buds** are the tiny bumps on your tongue that pick out sweet, salty, sour and bitter.

**Nerve** is the cable that carries messages inside your body. Nerves carry news from your senses to your brain, and commands back to your muscles.

**Stimulus** is the word for anything that sets off a sense. A bright light is a stimulus for your eyes, and a loud bang is one for your ears.
sections.heading: The Words We Use for the Senses

sections.body:
You can check how well your senses work with simple games. You only need things that are already at home.

To test your eyes, hold a pencil at arm's length. Close one eye. Move the pencil slowly towards your nose until it looks blurry. Then open that eye and close the other one. Whichever eye blurs last is your stronger eye.

To test your hearing, ask someone to stand behind you and clap once. See if you can tell which side the clap came from.

To test your smell, close your eyes and smell something from the kitchen with one nostril closed. Then swap. Is one nostril better than the other? Many people find out that it is.

To test your taste, put a little salt on your tongue, then a little sugar. Take a sip of water between them.

To test your touch, close your eyes and ask someone to touch your arm. Can you tell exactly where they touched you?

Then try one sense with your eyes closed. Can you find your way along the wall of your classroom? Does it feel different when you walk with your eyes open?

Write down what you find. Then test again in a week. You might be surprised how much your senses improve when you pay attention to them.
examples: My left eye blurs first, so my right eye is stronger.
I heard the clap on the right side.
With my eyes closed I bumped into the desk.
sections.heading: How to Test Your Senses
steps: Hold a pencil at arm's length and test each eye in turn.
Ask someone to clap behind you and guess the side it came from.
Smell something from the kitchen with one nostril closed.
Taste a little salt, then a little sugar, with water in between.
Close your eyes and ask someone to touch your arm.
Walk along a wall with your eyes closed, then with them open.

item.summary: You use your senses every minute of the day. After reading this, you can name the five senses, explain what each one does for you, and test your senses so you know how well they work.
item.title: Discovering the Five Senses
